content: Neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE) is a passively transferred autoimmune disease that occurs in approximately 1–2% of infants born to mothers with autoimmune conditions, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and Sjögren’s syndrome. This condition is associated with maternal antibodies to SSA/Ro and/or SSB/La. The most severe complication of neonatal lupus is complete heart block. The first documented case of neonatal lupus was reported by Aylward in 1928, describing two siblings with complete heart block born to a mother with Sjögren’s syndrome. In 1945, Plant and Stevens identified complete heart block as a manifestation of neonatal lupus. McCuistion and Schoch, in 1954, were the first to link maternal autoimmune disease with cutaneous lupus in the infant. Hogg, in 1957, suggested a possible relationship between maternal autoimmune disease and congenital heart block in offspring. Finally, in 1980, Weston established the association between neonatal lupus and maternal anti-Ro autoantibodies. The pathophysiology of neonatal lupus is believed to involve the transplacental transfer of maternal anti-SSA/Ro and/or anti-SSB/La antibodies. Ro and La molecules are thought to form a single particle present in all cells. Recent studies have explored the role of naturally acquired fetal and maternal microchimerism in autoimmune diseases, including neonatal lupus. During pregnancy, cell transfer between the mother and fetus can result in the long-term persistence of fetal cells in the mother (fetal microchimerism) and maternal cells in the offspring (maternal microchimerism). Maternal microchimerism has been identified in the hearts of male infants with neonatal lupus syndrome who died from congenital heart block. Genetic factors in the infant, such as specific HLA alleles (DQB102, DRB103) and a polymorphism in the promoter region of the tumor necrosis factor-alpha gene (-308A, associated with higher TNF-alpha production), may contribute to the development of skin disease in neonatal lupus. The primary cause of neonatal lupus is the presence of maternal antibodies that cross the placenta. These antibodies are responsible for 60–90% of cases of congenital complete heart block. Maternal antibodies to SSA/Ro and/or SSB/La are the most common culprits, but antibodies to other antigens, such as anti-U1 RNP antibodies, have also been implicated in rare cases. The role of fetal and maternal microchimerism in autoimmune diseases, including neonatal lupus, has been a focus of recent research. Differentiating neonatal lupus erythematosus from other diseases is important. In cases without neonatal lupus or significant congenital structural heart disease, familial inheritance of conduction disease is often responsible for atrioventricular (AV) block. The prevalence of anti-SSA antibodies in women is approximately 1 in 200, while the incidence of neonatal lupus is only 1 in 20,000 live births. The risk increases to 3% if the mother has anti-La antibodies in addition to anti-Ro antibodies. If the mother has SLE along with anti-SSA antibodies, the incidence of neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE) may rise to 6–13%. This risk is even higher, reaching up to 25%, if the mother has previously had a child with neonatal lupus. Among affected infants, 15–20% present with complete heart block, and 6% present with cutaneous lupus. Congenital heart block occurs in 50–60% of cases, cutaneous lupus in 25–30%, and a combination of cardiac and cutaneous manifestations in only 4–10% of patients with neonatal lupus. The most significant risk factor for congenital heart block is the presence of maternal antibodies to SSA/Ro and/or SSB/La. Other risk factors include maternal anti-U1 RNP antibodies and fetal or genetic factors. Prenatal screening for anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La antibodies is recommended for women at risk. Women more likely to have these antibodies include those with lupus, Sjögren’s syndrome, undifferentiated autoimmune disease, or a history of having a baby with neonatal lupus in a previous pregnancy. The natural history of neonatal lupus varies. The rash associated with neonatal lupus typically resolves without scarring within six to eight months. The appearance of skin lesions postnatally is independent of breastfeeding, and breastfeeding is not contraindicated in mothers with anti-SSA/Ro and/or anti-SSB/La antibodies. Infants and young children with asymptomatic complete heart block often remain well until later childhood, adolescence, or adulthood. However, exercise limitations and even death can occur without pacing. Prognosis following pacemaker implantation is excellent for most children, although heart failure may develop in some cases. Diagnosis of neonatal lupus involves identifying maternal anti-SSA/Ro and SSB/La autoantibodies. Pregnant women who test positive for these antibodies may benefit from frequent fetal echocardiographic testing to monitor for fetal heart block. Complete heart block, and often second-degree AV block, results in fetal bradycardia, which can be detected through routine fetal auscultation, ultrasonography, or echocardiography. Treatment options for neonatal lupus include medical therapy and surgical interventions. Prenatal treatment with fluorinated glucocorticoids is suggested for mothers of fetuses with second-degree heart block, continuing through the end of pregnancy depending on the response. Expert recommendations also suggest preemptive treatment with hydroxychloroquine (400 mg orally once daily) in pregnant women with anti-SSA/Ro antibodies who have previously given birth to a child with cardiac manifestations of neonatal lupus, regardless of the mother’s health status. The primary therapeutic decision after the immediate perinatal period involves determining the need for pacemaker placement.
